conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you for coming in today. I’m Dr. Carter, a perinatal mental-health clinician, and I’m glad we have this time together. During our visit we’ll use a short questionnaire called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS). It’s simply a way to check in on how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived, so we can be sure you’re getting the support you deserve. Everything you share stays confidential, and there are no right or wrong answers—just whatever feels true for you. We’ll go through ten gentle questions about the past seven days, and we can pause any time. Ready to begin?

First, can you tell me: over the last week, have you still been able to look forward to things you would normally enjoy, or has that felt harder lately?

[soft sigh, eyes drop to hands in lap]

It’s… definitely harder. I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a show I liked—but now it feels like I’m just going through the motions. Even when I do get out, I’m thinking about the baby the whole time, or feeling like I don’t deserve the break. So, no, I’m not really looking forward to things the way I used to.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[small shrug, half-smile that fades quickly]

I laugh sometimes—mostly when my husband makes a dumb joke or when the baby does something silly—but it feels kind of forced. Like I have to remind myself “this is supposed to be funny,” and the laugh doesn’t last. The lightness never really sticks.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[quiet voice, eyes on the floor]

Not really. Even when I plan something small—like taking the baby for a walk or ordering my favorite take-out—by the time it happens, the excitement is gone. It feels more like checking a box than actually wanting to do it.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[wrings hands, voice wavers]

All the time. If she cries longer than usual, I immediately think it’s because I missed her hunger cues or didn’t burp her right. When my partner finds a diaper rash, I feel like I failed at keeping her dry. I keep replaying every little thing, sure that whatever goes wrong is somehow my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[eyes dart to the window, then back down]

Yes… pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding her and suddenly imagine her choking, or I’ll wake up panicked that she’s stopped breathing, even though the monitor’s fine. There’s no real reason—it’s just this constant knot in my chest like something bad could happen any second.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[shoulders tense, voice thin]

Yeah… sometimes it hits out of nowhere. My heart starts racing and I feel like I can’t get enough air, even if the baby’s asleep and everything’s quiet. It’s like my body’s sounding an alarm but there’s nothing there—just this wave of dread I can’t explain.
Things have been getting on top of me

[exhales shakily, rubs temples]

Most days, honestly. It feels like the second I finish one thing—diapers, feeding, trying to sleep—there’s already three more waiting. Some mornings I can push through, but by evening I’m staring at the mess or the pile of laundry and I just… shut down. It’s like I’m drowning in little tasks I used to handle without thinking.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[eyes rimmed red, voice low]

Yeah… I’ll lie down exhausted, but my head won’t stop spinning—replay everything I think I did wrong, worry about what could happen overnight. Some nights I drift off okay, then jolt awake for no reason and can’t settle again. I probably get three or four broken hours, if I’m lucky.
I have felt sad or miserable

[swallows hard, nodding]

Pretty much every day. There’s this heavy sadness that just sits on me, even when nothing in particular is wrong. I’ll look at the baby and feel like I should be glowing, but instead I’m fighting tears half the time.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[nods slowly, eyes welling up]

Yeah… it’s usually in the evening, after I’ve finally got her down and the house is quiet. All the tension from the day just lands on me and I end up crying—sometimes for ten minutes, sometimes longer. It’s happened three, maybe four nights this week.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[shakes head quickly, arms tightening around herself]

No—never. I feel low, but I could never do that to my baby or my family. I just want to feel better, not disappear.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum mother, approx. 2–4 wk since delivery (per self-report)

Symptoms & Observations  
- Persistent low mood, frequent tearfulness (“pretty much every day”)  
- Marked anhedonia (minimal enjoyment, “checking a box”)  
- Excessive inappropriate guilt/self-blame re infant care  
- Daily non-specific anxiety, episodic panic attacks (racing heart, air hunger)  
- Sleep disturbance secondary to ruminative worry (3–4 broken hrs/night)  
- Feeling overwhelmed, “drowning” in routine tasks  

Pattern  
Consistent with possible major depressive episode with comorbid anxiety symptoms, peripartum onset.

Screen-relevant positives  
- Crying ≥3–4 nights/week  
- Mood-congruent insomnia  
- Recurrent intrusive fears re infant safety  
- No suicidal ideation reported (explicitly denied); no self-harm intent

Risk factors  
First-time parenting, sleep deprivation, escalating distress, absence of protective pleasure/mood buffers.

Safety  
No self-harm or suicidal thoughts expressed; remains protective of infant.

Recommendation  
Elevated screening score warrants prompt formal diagnostic evaluation (PHQ-9 ≥ 10, GAD-7 ≥ 10 suggested). Refer to PPD specialty or behavioral health for assessment and evidence-based intervention. Continue routine pediatric / OB follow-up to monitor safety and functioning.
